accused_occupation: Irregular casual jobs for sustenance (no specific occupation stated)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (murder); defence of insanity under IPC s.84 raised by accused
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW1, PW5 and neighbours), medical (post-mortem, PW9), recovery (chopper and clothing seized), forensic (blood group report), circumstantial
confession: Oral extra-judicial confession to neighbours, as alleged by PW5; the Supreme Court did not expressly rely on it
aggravating_circumstances: Brutal, callous killing with chopper on victim's neck; nine injuries; wounds on victim's palm and fingers indicating she was defending herself and attacked while awake
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction under s.302 IPC affirmed
neutral_facts: The victim was found dead in a bedroom of the accused's house on the evening of 3 November 2000, with a neck wound inflicted by a chopper. The prosecution case was that at about 7.30 p.m. the accused struck the victim on the neck with a chopper while she was in the bedroom. The accused then left the house and approached two neighbours sitting in front of their house, carrying the couple's eight-month-old child in one arm and a chopper in the other hand. One neighbour stepped towards the accused to take the child and saw the chopper. The neighbour and his son went inside and closed the door. Through the window, the son shone a torch and saw the accused's shirt stained with blood and a blood-stained chopper in hand. The accused asked another neighbour to look after the child, said he was going to the police station, and later put the chopper on the verandah floor when asked. He entrusted the child to a third neighbour and went away. Neighbours entered the house and found the victim lying on a cot, covered in blood, with no movement. The accused had told neighbours he had killed the victim. The post-mortem certificate recorded nine incised wounds on the victim's head, neck, ear, shoulders, back, and hand, including wounds on the palm and fingers. The doctor said the injuries could have been caused by the seized chopper. Blood-stained items were sent for forensic examination and found to contain human blood of group A. The chopper and clothing were seized and an FIR was registered on the basis of a neighbour's statement.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from nine incised wounds, including a deep incised wound on the back of the neck severing the vertebral column
number_of_offences: 1 charged (IPC s.302 is the only offence of conviction; charge sheet not quoted); 1 finally upheld
motive: alleged: accused's suspicion that the wife had been unfaithful, per the accused's remark recounted by PW2; not decided by the court
key_evidence_accepted: Ocular evidence of PW1 and PW5 (accused approaching with blood-stained chopper and child; torchlight sighting); PW3's account of blood on body; PW9 post-mortem evidence that injuries could be caused by the seized chopper
witness_credibility: High Court found PW1 to PW5 unimpeachable; Supreme Court accepted that ocular evidence was corroborated by medical evidence and gave no reason to disturb this
post_offence_conduct: Carried the blood-stained chopper, confessed to neighbours, left the child in a neighbour's care and went away; court found he arranged proper care for the child after the murder
trial_duration: offence: 3.11.2000; trial judgment: 30.11.2002; High Court: 21.10.2005; Supreme Court: 26.10.2010 (judgment date; hearing date not given)
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: T.V. George, Manjula Gupta; State/respondent: Shishir Pinaki, P.V. Dinesh
investigation_status: FIR registered on PW1's statement; accused arrested by Circle Inspector; inquest, seizure and forensic examination conducted; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment (30.11.2002); High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction affirmed (21.10.2005); Supreme Court: appeal dismissed (26.10.2010)
prosecution_argument: Not stated (the judgment records only the accused's submissions; the Supreme Court accepted the courts below's findings on the evidence)
defence_argument: Story unbelievable given the densely populated locality; defence wrongly discarded; accused suffered paranoid schizophrenia, shown by records treated 11 days after the incident and by medical witnesses; schizophrenia causes rapid emotional change so the accused could not be said to be in his senses at the time
legal_principle_applied: Under IPC s.84 the accused must show that, at the time of the offence, unsoundness of mind rendered him incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law; burden on accused under Evidence Act s.105 is no higher than in civil proceedings; prosecution must prove mens rea beyond reasonable doubt
precedent_relied_upon: Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat AIR 1964 SC 1563; Ratan Lal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1970) 3 SCC 533; R. v. Daniel McNaughten (1843) 8 ER 718 (HL)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal and callous commission of the murder of the wife
